lines: A pipeline is many sorts, joins and loads, with dependencies between them. Graph algorithms decide their order, catch cycles, and find what sets the finish time.
So draw the shop's pipeline the way an engineer would on a whiteboard. Every task is a dot, and every arrow says: this must finish before that starts.
Once it is a picture, a lot of scheduling questions turn into questions about a picture.
Two properties make this particular graph easy to work with. Look at the arrows first.
They point one way. A dependency is not symmetric: clean must finish before load, and load does not have to finish before clean.
And follow any arrow chain forward. It never returns to where it began, because a task that waits on itself could never start.
A graph with those two properties is a DAG, and it is the shape nearly every scheduler assumes before it will run anything.
Here is a question you will be asked at two in the morning. You just changed the cleaning step.
Look at the graph and think about which direction the damage travels.
Which tasks have to run again?
answer: Everything the cleaning step feeds, directly or through others: load orders, the metrics branch, daily revenue and publish.
Ingest and the customer load sit above the change, so they are untouched. That is why only clean itself is too little, and why every task is too much.
Only the immediate successor misses the tasks further down. The rule is to walk the arrows forward as far as they go.

lines: That forward walk has a mirror image. Walk the same arrows backwards, and you find what a task depends on.
That is the set a backfill needs. To rebuild daily revenue you need the ingest, the clean, the orders and the customers.
Both are one traversal, whether breadth first or depth first, and each visits every vertex and edge once.
So the cost grows with the number of tasks plus the number of arrows. A pipeline ten times bigger is ten times the work, not a hundred.
Now, in what order do you actually run them? Keep one number per task: how many of its dependencies have not finished. That is its in-degree.
Start everything with a count of zero. Each time a task finishes, subtract one from every task it feeds.
Whatever reaches zero is ready, and it joins the queue. That is Kahn's algorithm.
The useful part is what you get for free. Release the whole ready queue at once and you have the waves of parallel work a scheduler launches.
Use the counts to predict the schedule. Ingest and the customer load have nothing to wait on, so they open the first wave.
From there, follow the zeros as they appear. Each wave is whatever became ready when the last one finished.
How many waves does the whole pipeline take?
answer: Five. The two roots, then clean, then load orders and the metrics branch together, then daily revenue, then publish.
The width of each wave is the parallelism you actually have at that moment. Seven waves would mean no two tasks ever overlap, and three would skip a dependency.
One wave is impossible, because publish needs the whole chain before it. Python's standard library does this bookkeeping for you.

lines: What if someone wires a loop by mistake? Think about the counts. Every task in the loop is waiting on another task in the loop.
So none of them ever reaches zero, and no valid order exists.
Kahn's algorithm notices when tasks are left stuck above zero. A depth first walk notices the moment it steps back onto a task already on its own path.
A good orchestrator runs this check before anything starts. A cycle becomes an error at import time, not a hang at three in the morning.
Last idea, and the most useful. Give yourself all the workers you want. When does the pipeline finish?
Not the sum of all the tasks, because they overlap. And not the longest chain counted in tasks, because tasks differ in length.
It is the longest path when each task is weighted by its duration. That is the critical path.
Now the quiet surprise. Finding a longest path is usually brutally hard. On a DAG it is one sweep in dependency order, because acyclicity means you never have to revisit a vertex.
Put numbers on it. The revenue branch runs about fifty five minutes end to end. The metrics branch runs sixty two.
So the pipeline finishes at sixty two, and the metrics branch is the critical one.
Now load orders sits on the revenue branch. You make it twice as fast.
By how much does the finish time move?
answer: That branch has slack. It was never setting the finish time, so shaving it only gives you more slack.

A few minutes sooner and exactly as much as you saved both assume every task matters equally. Only a task on the critical path moves the clock, and cut it far enough and the path shifts to the other branch.
Which workers are available does not change this, since we assumed enough of them.

lines: One more lens. Tasks that share no dependency, even indirectly, form separate components.
They can run on different workers, fail without affecting each other, and belong to different teams.

Finding them is one more walk over the graph. And that is the pattern for this whole topic: order the tasks, catch the cycle, trace what reruns, find what sets the clock, all linear in the size of the graph.
The tasks of a DAG run on many machines. Next: what the network between them costs, in bandwidth, latency and where the data lives.
